metadata.disclaimer: This information is for general educational guidance only. Disease management practices vary by region, season, and local regulations. Always follow label instructions and seek advice from a qualified local agricultural expert before applying any treatment. No specific product names or doses are provided intentionally.

diseases.summary: Bacterial disease causing dark, water-soaked spots on leaves, stems, and fruit. Spreads rapidly in warm, wet conditions.
symptoms: Small, dark brown to black water-soaked spots on leaves
Spots often have yellow halos
Leaf edges may appear ragged or torn
Raised, scab-like lesions on green fruit
Severe infection causes defoliation
favorable_conditions: High humidity and frequent rain or overhead irrigation
Plant wounds from pruning or insects

cultural: Use certified disease-free or treated seeds [S01, S07]
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation where possible [S02, S07]
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest [S01, S06]
Rotate crops — avoid tomato and pepper in the same field for at least 2 years [S03, S07]
Stake and prune plants to improve airflow [S02]
Avoid working in the field when foliage is wet [S05]
biological: Copper-based bactericides (copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride) applied preventively can reduce spread — follow local extension recommendations for timing and number of applications [S01, S02, S03]
Note: copper resistance in Xanthomonas has been reported; consult your local KVK or extension officer [S06]
chemical_groups: Copper-based compounds (copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, copper sulfate) — apply preventively [S01, S02, S03]
Always follow the label and local advice; resistance management is important [S06]
management.resistant_varieties: Several bacterial spot-tolerant tomato varieties are available; consult your local seed supplier or KVK [S01, S07]

diseases.summary: Common fungal disease producing characteristic concentric-ring ('target') lesions on older leaves first. Can cause significant defoliation and fruit loss.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older/lower leaves
Yellow (chlorotic) area surrounding lesions
Lesions on stems appear dark and sunken
Fruit lesions are dark, leathery, and sunken near the stem end
Defoliation progresses upward from older leaves
favorable_conditions: Plant stress (nutrient deficiency, drought, heavy fruit load)

cultural: Remove and destroy infected leaves and crop debris [S01, S02]
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base of the plant [S03]
Maintain adequate plant nutrition, especially nitrogen and potassium [S05, S07]
Mulch to reduce soil splash onto lower leaves [S02, S03]
Crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops for 2–3 years [S01, S07]
Stake plants to improve airflow [S02]
biological: Trichoderma-based biocontrol agents can be used as soil drenches or seed treatments — available through ICAR-recommended formulations [S07, S09]
chemical_groups: Mancozeb (dithiocarbamate group) — broad-spectrum protectant [S01, S02]
Chlorothalonil (chloronitrile group) — protectant [S03, S05]
Azoxystrobin or other strobilurins — systemic; use in rotation with other groups to avoid resistance [S02, S06]
Always follow the label and local advice for number of applications and pre-harvest intervals [S01]
management.resistant_varieties: Moderate resistance available in some varieties; check with local seed suppliers or ICAR recommendations [S01, S07]

diseases.summary: Highly destructive water-mould disease capable of destroying an entire crop within days under favorable conditions. The same pathogen caused the Irish Potato Famine.
symptoms: Large, irregular, pale green to brown water-soaked lesions on leaves
White, powdery/downy sporulation visible on the underside of lesions in humid conditions
Dark brown, greasy lesions on stems
Brown, firm, greasy rot on fruit — may have white mold on surface
Rapid collapse and death of affected tissue
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (10–24°C) combined with high humidity (>90%)

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plant material immediately — do not compost [S02, S05]
Avoid overhead irrigation [S03]
Space plants adequately and stake to improve airflow [S02]
Scout fields frequently during cool, wet weather [S05, S06]
Avoid planting near potato fields [S06]
Destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants [S03]
biological: Copper-based fungicides have some activity and can be used in an IPM program — apply preventively when conditions favor the disease [S01, S03]
chemical_groups: Copper-based compounds (copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride) — protectant, apply preventively [S01, S02]
Mancozeb (dithiocarbamate) — protectant [S01, S03]
Metalaxyl or mefenoxam (phenylamide group) — systemic; MUST be rotated with other groups to prevent resistance [S02, S06]
Mandipropamid or dimethomorph (CAA group) — systemic [S06]
Always follow the label and local advice; resistance to metalaxyl is widespread in some regions [S06]
management.resistant_varieties: Varieties with Ph-2 and Ph-3 genes offer partial resistance; consult your local seed supplier or ICAR recommendations [S01, S07]

diseases.summary: Fungal disease mainly affecting leaves; most problematic in greenhouse and high-humidity conditions. Causes yield loss through defoliation.
symptoms: Pale green or yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to brown or purple-grey velvety mold on the underside of leaves
Infected leaves curl, turn brown, and drop
Rarely affects fruit directly in the field
favorable_conditions: Poor ventilation — especially in greenhouse or poly-house cultivation

cultural: Improve ventilation in greenhouses and poly-houses [S02, S06]
Avoid overhead irrigation; reduce leaf wetness duration [S03]
Remove and destroy infected leaves [S02]
Keep plant density adequate to allow airflow [S06]
Sanitize greenhouse structures between crops [S02]
biological: Biocontrol agents based on Trichoderma or Bacillus subtilis may help as part of an IPM program [S07, S09]
chemical_groups: Mancozeb (dithiocarbamate) — protectant [S01]
Chlorothalonil (chloronitrile) — protectant [S03]
Strobilurin group (e.g., azoxystrobin) — systemic; rotate to avoid resistance [S06]
Always follow the label and local advice [S01]
management.resistant_varieties: Varieties with Cf resistance genes are available and highly effective; consult your local seed supplier [S02, S06]

diseases.summary: Common fungal disease causing numerous small circular spots, leading to defoliation from the bottom of the plant upward. Can significantly reduce fruit quality.
symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots (3–6 mm) with dark brown margins and lighter grey centres
Tiny black dots (pycnidia — fungal fruiting bodies) visible in the centre of spots
Affects lower/older leaves first; progresses upward
Severely affected leaves turn yellow and drop
Does not typically infect fruit directly

cultural: Remove and destroy infected leaves and crop debris [S01, S05]
Avoid overhead irrigation [S02, S03]
Mulch to reduce soil splash [S02]
Crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops [S01, S07]
Stake plants to improve airflow [S02]
Avoid working in wet fields [S05]
biological: Trichoderma-based products may be used as part of an IPM program [S07, S09]
chemical_groups: Mancozeb (dithiocarbamate) — protectant; apply preventively [S01, S02]
Chlorothalonil (chloronitrile) — protectant [S03, S05]
Strobilurin group — systemic; rotate to avoid resistance [S06]
Always follow the label and local advice [S01]
management.resistant_varieties: Limited genetic resistance available; focus on cultural controls [S05, S06]

diseases.pathogen: Tetranychus urticae (arthropod pest — not a fungal or bacterial disease)
diseases.summary: Tiny sap-sucking mites that cause stippling and bronzing of leaves. Not a disease but included because PlantVillage includes them in tomato disease classification.
symptoms: Fine stippling (tiny pale dots) on the upper leaf surface
Leaves turn pale, bronze, or silvery
Fine webbing on undersides of leaves and between leaves
Severe infestations cause leaf drop and plant decline
Tiny moving dots (mites) visible on undersides of leaves with a hand lens
favorable_conditions: Overuse of broad-spectrum pesticides that kill natural enemies

cultural: Monitor fields regularly, especially during hot, dry spells [S02, S07]
Maintain adequate irrigation to reduce plant stress [S02]
Remove heavily infested leaves [S05]
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes lush growth favorable to mites [S03]
Maintain ground cover and weed management to support natural predators [S07]
biological: Predatory mites (Phytoseiidae family, e.g., Phytoseiulus persimilis, Neoseiulus californicus) are natural enemies and effective biocontrol agents [S02, S07]
Neem-based products (azadirachtin) have miticidal activity and are compatible with natural enemies [S01, S07]
Releasing or conserving predatory mites is recommended in IPM programs [S07]
chemical_groups: Abamectin (avermectin group) — miticide/insecticide; use judiciously to preserve natural enemies [S02, S03]
Spiromesifen or bifenazate — specific miticides; rotate groups to prevent resistance [S06]
Avoid broad-spectrum organophosphates and pyrethroids where possible — they kill natural predators [S07]
Always follow the label and local advice [S01]
management.resistant_varieties: No commercially available spider mite-resistant tomato varieties; management relies on cultural and biological controls [S03]

diseases.summary: Fungal disease producing concentric-ring lesions similar to early blight but with distinguishing features. Can affect leaves, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings (target pattern) on leaves
Spots lack the distinct yellow halo typical of early blight
Dark brown, sunken lesions on stems and petioles
Dark brown, slightly sunken lesions on fruit
Defoliation under severe infection

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plant debris [S02, S08]
Avoid overhead irrigation [S03]
Stake and prune to improve airflow [S02]
Crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops [S08]
Mulch to reduce soil splash [S02]
biological: Trichoderma-based biocontrol agents may provide some suppression as part of an IPM program [S07, S09]
chemical_groups: Mancozeb (dithiocarbamate) — protectant [S08]
Chlorothalonil (chloronitrile) — protectant [S08]
Strobilurin group — systemic; rotate to avoid resistance [S06, S08]
Always follow the label and local advice [S01]
management.resistant_varieties: Limited information on resistant varieties; cultural management is the primary strategy [S08]

diseases.pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (begomovirus, transmitted by Bemisia tabaci whitefly)
diseases.summary: Devastating viral disease transmitted by whiteflies. No cure once a plant is infected; management focuses on preventing infection and controlling the whitefly vector.
symptoms: Upward curling and cupping of young leaves
Yellowing (chlorosis) of leaf margins and between veins
Stunted plant growth
Reduced leaf size
Flowers may drop; fruit set severely reduced if infection occurs early
Silvery-white whiteflies visible on undersides of leaves
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry conditions that favor whitefly multiplication
Presence of infected host plants near the field

cultural: Use certified TYLCV-resistant or tolerant varieties — this is the most effective long-term strategy [S01, S07]
Use reflective silver or yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce whitefly populations [S02, S07]
Use insect-proof netting in nurseries to raise healthy transplants [S01, S07]
Rogue out and destroy infected plants as soon as symptoms appear — do not leave them in the field [S02, S07]
Remove crop debris immediately after harvest [S01]
Avoid planting near older tomato crops or other whitefly host plants [S06, S07]
Plant border crops (such as maize or sorghum) as physical barriers [S07]
biological: Natural enemies of whiteflies (parasitic wasps such as Encarsia formosa, predatory beetles) can be conserved or released as biocontrol [S07]
Neem-based products reduce whitefly populations and are compatible with natural enemies [S01, S07]
chemical_groups: Neonicotinoid group (e.g., imidacloprid, thiamethoxam) — systemic insecticides against whitefly; use judiciously due to resistance and pollinator concerns [S02, S07]
Pyrethroid group — contact insecticide; rotation recommended to manage resistance [S07]
NOTE: Insecticides control the vector (whitefly) but cannot cure infected plants [S01, S02]
Always follow the label and local advice; whitefly resistance to insecticides is a growing problem [S06, S07]
management.resistant_varieties: TYLCV-resistant varieties are strongly recommended and are the most effective management tool; consult your local seed supplier or ICAR/SAU recommendations [S01, S07]

diseases.summary: Highly stable virus that spreads through contact, tools, and infected plant material. No cure; management focuses on prevention and sanitation.
symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green on leaves
Leaf distortion, curling, and puckering
Stunted plant growth
Mottled or streaked fruit
Fruit may show internal browning
Symptoms may be mild in some conditions
favorable_conditions: Handling plants without sanitation (virus spreads easily on hands, tools, clothing)
Presence of infected weed hosts near the field
Tobacco use by field workers (tobacco may carry related tobamoviruses)

cultural: Use certified virus-free or heat-treated seed [S01, S02]
Wash hands thoroughly with soap before handling plants and between rows [S02, S05]
Disinfect tools and equipment between plants (10% bleach solution or appropriate disinfectant) [S02, S05]
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately [S01, S05]
Control weed hosts in and around the field [S07]
Avoid tobacco products near tomato plants [S05, S06]
Do not save seed from infected plants [S02]
biological: No effective biological control agents available; prevention through sanitation is essential [S05, S06]
chemical_groups: No chemical treatments are effective against the virus itself [S05, S06]
Management is entirely through cultural and sanitation practices [S01, S02]
management.resistant_varieties: Varieties with Tm-2 and Tm-2a genes offer good resistance to ToMV; consult your local seed supplier or ICAR/SAU recommendations [S01, S02, S07]

diseases.summary: No disease detected. The leaf appears healthy.

cultural: Continue regular scouting (at least twice a week) for early disease detection [S02, S07]
Maintain balanced nutrition and irrigation [S01, S07]
Keep records of any unusual symptoms for early intervention [S07]
management.resistant_varieties: Using disease-resistant varieties is recommended as a preventive measure for all major tomato diseases [S01, S07]
